title: Whoever is least (Luke 9:37–50)
hook: a boy healed, an argument about greatness, a child set beside him

segments.voice: Yesterday, a mountain, a changed face, and Moses and Elijah talking about an exodus. Your line was while he prayed. Did you stay in the quiet a little longer? Day five hundred thirty-seven.

The next day they come down the mountain, and a crowd is waiting, and a father is shouting over the noise. "Master, I beseech thee, look upon my son: for he is mine only child." Luke says a spirit seizes the boy, throws him into convulsions and leaves him bruised. And the father adds the painful part: "I besought thy disciples to cast him out; and they could not." The disciples who stayed below have failed in front of everyone. Jesus' answer is weary, almost a sigh at the whole generation: how long shall I be with you? Then, simply: "Bring thy son hither."
screen: `LOOK UPON MY SON: MINE ONLY CHILD.`

segments.voice: Even as the boy is brought, he's thrown down again. Jesus rebukes the spirit, heals the child, and, in the King James words, "delivered him again to his father." Gave him back. The same gesture as the widow's son at Nain. The crowd is "amazed at the mighty power of God." And while everyone is marveling, Jesus tells his disciples something hard: the Son of man will be delivered into human hands. They don't understand, and they're afraid to ask. Then, Luke says, a strange thing: "there arose a reasoning among them, which of them should be greatest." Right after failing to heal a boy. Right after hearing their teacher will be handed over. They argue about rank. Jesus knows what they're thinking, and he answers without a speech. He "took a child, and set him by him." Next to himself. The disciples have been arguing about rank, and a child has none to offer. And he says: "Whosoever shall receive this child in my name receiveth me: and whosoever shall receive me receiveth him that sent me: for he that is least among you all, the same shall be great." Welcome this child, and you welcome Jesus, and the one who sent him. Then John, a little too quickly, reports: we saw someone driving out demons in your name, and we stopped him, because he isn't one of us. Jesus: "Forbid him not: for he that is not against us is for us." Two lessons in a row against the same instinct: to rank people, and to guard the circle.
screen: then, large: `HE THAT IS LEAST AMONG YOU ALL, THE SAME SHALL BE GREAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: put a child's need first. Settle, and breathe. Picture Jesus taking a child by the hand and setting them next to him, while the grown-ups go quiet. Now think of a child in your life: your own, a niece or nephew, a neighbor's kid, a student, a child you sponsor, or the child you once were. What do they need right now that's easy to overlook because adult things feel more urgent? Time. Attention. A meal, a ride, a bedtime story, a promise kept. Let one need come clearly. Then picture putting it first today, ahead of something that seemed more important. If you pray, you can hold that child before God. If you don't, simply hold them in mind with care. The bell holds the time.

John. One of the twelve, who tried to stop a stranger driving out demons in Jesus's name, and was told not to forbid him. That same day, Jesus set a child beside him and said the least among you is the one who is great.
Your line: the least is the greatest. Today, put one child's need ahead of something that felt more important, and notice who gets the seat beside you. Day five hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Some churches point to Luke 9:48 in their work with children, from Sunday schools to child-protection and welcome policies, as a sign that receiving a child is receiving Jesus.

fork.setup: your friends are arguing about which of them is the greatest. you're their teacher. what do you do?
options: give a long talk on humility.
take a child, set the child beside you, and say the least is great.
name the greatest to end the argument.
fork.reveal: Jesus doesn't argue. he sets a child next to himself and says whoever welcomes this child welcomes him.

original.note: Greek: smaller, lesser, least. "he that is least among you all."

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus liked children.
what it means: he sets a child next to himself while the disciples argue about rank, and turns the disciples' idea of greatness upside down.
what a scholar hears: Luke calls three people in his healing stories an "only" child, monogenes: the widow's son, Jairus's daughter and this boy.

notes: 'A child had no status of their own then' is a broad historical claim; Keeper may soften.
monogenes in Luke 7:12, 8:42 and 9:38 (only Luke uses it in these healing stories). Confirm.
The boy's seizures: Luke describes a spirit that throws him down; the script stays with Luke's description.
KJV 9:50 'not against us is for us' (some manuscripts read 'you'). Confirm.
